deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. The previous page defines determinants of n×n systems in Gauss's notation. (pq) is the element with first index p (horizontal position, i.e. column) and second index q (row). (abc…, αβγ…) is the determinant of the subsystem with columns a,b,c,… and rows α,β,γ…. Gauss announces three theorems ('drei Lehrsätze'), stated for a 5×5 system 'for simplicity' but 'easily generalised'. This page gives them, then a separate note on the binomial mean error.

Modern notation: A = (a_{rc}) with a_{rc} = Gauss's (c r), and A[R;C] is the minor with row set R and column set C. Gauss's (C,R) = det A[R;C].

THEOREM I.
(01234,01234) = (0123,0123)(44) − (0124,0123)(34) + (0134,0123)(24) − (0234,0123)(14) + (1234,0123)(04).
Modern form: det A = Σ_{k=0}^{4} (−1)^{k+4} a_{4k} det A[{0,1,2,3}; {0..4}∖{k}].
This is cofactor (Laplace) expansion along the last row (row 4). Each element (k4) multiplies the 4×4 minor on rows 0–3 with column k deleted, with alternating signs starting with + at (44).

Crossed-out start: '(01234,01234)(0123,0123) =' is an abandoned first version of II, deleting rows/columns 3,4 instead of 0,1 (Gauss's deletion).

THEOREM II.
(01234,01234)(234,234) = (0234,0234)(1234,1234) − (0234,1234)(1234,0234).
Modern form, with A^{i}_{j} = A with row i and column j removed:
det A · det A^{01}_{01} = det A^{1}_{1} · det A^{0}_{0} − det A^{0}_{1} · det A^{1}_{0}.
- (0234,1234) has columns 0234 and rows 1234, i.e. row 0 and column 1 deleted.
- (1234,0234) has row 1 and column 0 deleted.
This is the Desnanot–Jacobi identity (Sylvester's determinant identity, the 2×2 case; Dodgson condensation). The determinant times the doubly bordered-off central minor equals the 2×2 determinant of the four 'corner' minors.

THEOREM III. Blotted at the start and with no equality sign. The most plausible reading of the first factor is (1234,1234) (my reading). The line is then
(1234,1234)(234,034) − (1234,0234)(234,134) − (1234,0134)(234,234).
Let B = the 5×4 submatrix on columns 1–4 and C = the 5×3 submatrix on columns 2–4. With B_{î} = det of B without row i and C_{i34} = det C[{i,3,4}], the terms are B_{0̂}C_{034}, B_{1̂}C_{134}, B_{2̂}C_{234}.
The true identity (my completion) is B_{0̂}C_{034} − B_{1̂}C_{134} + B_{2̂}C_{234} = 0. Gauss's line is consistent with this if read as 'A − B = −C', the third term on the next line being the right-hand side.
Proof sketch (mine):
1. Extend the sum to i = 3, 4; those terms vanish because C_{i34} then has a repeated row. So E = Σ_{i=0}^{4} (−1)^i B_{î} C_{i34}.
2. Expand C_{i34} = Σ_k c_{ik} γ_k along row i.
3. Then E = Σ_k γ_k Σ_i (−1)^i b_{ik} B_{î}. The inner sum is the 5×5 determinant [column k of B | B], which has a repeated column, so it is 0.
This vanishing 'Plücker/Sylvester-type' relation between products of complementary minors is the standard lemma used to prove II.

PROBABILITY NOTE.
P(A) = α, P(B) = β = 1 − α. In n trials one expects αn occurrences of A and βn of B (= not A). The 'mittlere Fehler' (mean error, i.e. standard deviation) of this expectation is √(αβn).
Example: α = β = 1/2, n = 10^6 gives 500000 ± 500 as mean error (E. med.), since √(¼·10^6) = 500.
Next line: ½·1000000 ± 673, labelled 'E. veris'/'E. prob.' (reading uncertain). The probable error should be 0.67449·500 ≈ 337. 673 ≈ 2×337 ≈ 674.5, i.e. the full width of the probable-error interval, or 0.6745·√n with √n in place of √(n/4). See errors.
errors: III as written lacks an equality sign. If read as 'A − B − C = 0' the sign of the last term is wrong; the correct relation is A − B + C = 0, i.e. A − B = −C. A numeric check with a near-identity 5×4 matrix gives A = x2, B = 0, C = −x2.
In III the blotted first factor, transcribed '(0234,1234)', cannot be right: it would use column 0 while all other 4-minors use columns 1234. The consistent reading is (1234,1234).

'± 673' does not equal the probable error for σ = 500, which is 0.674490·500 ≈ 337.2. 673 is roughly twice that (≈674.5) or 0.6745·√n; either a slip (factor 2 or wrong variance) or a different quantity than the probable error. 673 also differs slightly from 674.5.
Theorems I and II are correct as written.

results.what: Expansion of a 5×5 determinant along the last row by 4×4 minors with alternating signs (Theorem I)
results.usually_credited_to: Laplace 1772 (general Laplace expansion); Vandermonde 1771; Cauchy 1812 systematic

results.what: det A · det A^{01}_{01} = A^0_0 A^1_1 − A^0_1 A^1_0 for 5×5, said to generalise easily (Theorem II)
results.modern_name: Desnanot–Jacobi identity / Sylvester's determinant identity (Dodgson condensation)
results.usually_credited_to: Desnanot 1819 (n ≤ 6), Jacobi 1833/1841 (general), Sylvester 1851, Dodgson 1866; 3×3 cases in Lagrange 1773

results.what: Vanishing alternating sum of products of complementary 4×4 and 3×3 minors of a 5×4 array (Theorem III, as corrected)
results.modern_name: Plücker-type (Grassmann–Plücker / Sylvester) quadratic relation among minors; lemma for Desnanot–Jacobi

results.what: Standard deviation of the number of successes in n Bernoulli trials is √(αβn); example 10^6 fair trials gives ±500

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's familiarity with elimination identities is known from his least-squares work, and he coined 'Determinante' (for forms). A systematic treatment of n×n determinants in index-pair notation with the Desnanot–Jacobi identity would be a notable unpublished detail, especially if dated near 1809, i.e. before Cauchy 1812 and Desnanot 1819. The dating is uncertain; the bundle name need not date this page, and the hand and notation may be later. The identities themselves were known in special cases (Lagrange) and the binomial part is routine, so the surprise is moderate at most.

Mean error √(αβn) = 500 for α = β = 1/2, n = 10^6
Probable error for σ = 500 is ≈ 337.2, not 673

transcription_corrections: Theorem I: '(4,4)' and the other elements are (34), (24), (14), (04); first index is column, second is row, consistent with the previous page.
Theorem III: the blotted first factor is most likely '(1234,1234)', not '(0234,1234)'; there is no visible '=' sign; the vertical stroke before the third term is an alignment or correction mark.
The probabilities are α and 'b'/β as transcribed ('e' in the image is Gauss's β).
'n = 1000 000' is written with a long tail of zeros; the value 10^6 is correct.
'E. veris' is uncertain; possibly an abbreviation such as 'E. prob.' (error probabilis) or 'E. verisim.'; the numeral clearly reads 673.
